title: What is Brahman?
hookLine: Arjuna fires off seven questions in a row, and the last one is about the moment of death
carry: remember God at all times, and act

cards: A teacher uses five unfamiliar words in one sentence. Everyone else nods. One student finally raises a hand.
That's Arjuna at the start of chapter eight. Krishna has just dropped a string of big terms: Brahman, the self, action. And Arjuna doesn't nod.
He asks, one after another: What is Brahman? What is the self? What is action?
And then the question underneath all the others: at the time of death, how are you known?

teach.b: Krishna answers fast, one line each.

Brahman, verse three, is the imperishable, the highest. The word akshara, imperishable, also means a syllable, a letter, something that can't be broken down further. The self, adhyatma, is one's own essential nature.

Action, karma, is the creative outpouring that brings beings into existence. Then the perishable world of things, the cosmic person behind the gods, and the Lord of sacrifice: Krishna himself, here, in this body.
That's the dictionary. Then comes the part people remember. Verse five: whoever, at the time of the end, leaves the body remembering me alone, comes to my being.
There's no doubt about it. Verse six widens it: whatever state a person remembers at the end, as they leave the body, to that state they go, because they've always been shaped by it.
So the moment of death isn't a pop quiz. It's the sum of what you've been practicing all along. Which is why verse seven, the closing line of this section, is so practical.
Therefore, at all times, remember me, and fight.

teach.h: WHAT YOU REMEMBER AT THE END.
teach.b: Not remember instead of living; remember while living.

teach.h: AT ALL TIMES, REMEMBER, AND FIGHT.
teach.b: Hindus call this smarana, remembering, and it's why many keep a name of God going under their breath all day, a practice called japa, often counted on a string of beads, a mala.
Arjuna is still standing between two armies. Krishna doesn't tell him to go meditate in a cave until he dies. He says: keep me in mind, and do what's in front of you.

how: Some Hindus practice smarana, the constant remembering of God, by repeating a divine name through the day, and some families chant God's name at the bedside of someone who is dying, in the spirit of Gita 8.5–8.7.

games.q: Krishna says what you remember at death shapes where you go. so what does he tell Arjuna to do now?
o: leave the battle and meditate until death.
at all times remember me, and fight.
don't think about death at all.
games.why: remember, and fight. keep him in mind while doing what's in front of you.

practice: Verse six says we become what we're shaped by, so look at what comes to mind most often when your mind is free, a worry, a person, a screen, and don't judge it.
Then choose one thing you'd like to be shaped by: a name of God if you pray, a person you love, a line from this path. Return to it on every breath.

wordCard.voice: Akshara. Imperishable, also a syllable, a letter, something that can't be broken down further. Krishna's first definition of Brahman, the highest.

orig.note: Sanskrit: akshara, imperishable; also a syllable or letter. Krishna's first definition of Brahman (8.3).

carryVoice: Your line: remember God at all times, and act. In the middle of everything, not instead of it. Day one hundred eighty-six.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 8.5–8.7 (remember me at the end, and at all times)
